newsitem.title: UK: Traders bearish despite slim early N.Sea programme.
newsitem.headline: Traders bearish despite slim early N.Sea programme.

text.p: North Sea crude oil traders remained bearish despite a lower than expected June Oseberg loading programme but said the market may hold up in the short term depending on how light first decade June loadings of Brent and Forties are.

"I still think it is going to come off. The U.S. stock build is bearish and refiners have built up stocks here over the past few weeks. Fundamentally we are not looking good," one North Sea producer said.
In the short term a possible light loading schedule on Forties and/or Brent in the first 10 days of June could hold differentials steady.
"I'm bearish overall but there are worries about early June. That's why I'm interested in seeing the Forties schedule," another commented.
The June loading programmes for Brent and Forties were not expected to be released until Thursday.
Wednesday's lighter than expected June Oseberg schedule was not particularly market supportive, they said.
June Oseberg loadings are down from 44.2 average 500,000 barrel cargoes in May to 30.7 average sized cargoes in June.

"It's less than expected but not that important. The European refiners are fairly relaxed," another trader said adding that he had expected to see Oseberg loadings down by 10 cargoes due to upcoming field maintenance.
Overnight weekly U.S. stock figures from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed a crude build of almost seven million barrels with gasoline up 6.5 million barrels.
Although traders said the numbers overall looked suspect with crude stocks up dramatically while refinery runs rose and crude imports fell, the story was one of high stocks.
"The Americans look to me like they have enough," another North Sea producer said.
Traders said that buying from the East which, had been expected to mop up most of the West African barrels, was lighter than expected.
"The pull from the East is less than expected. The margins there are not great and gas oil is not as hyped in the East as it was," one trader of West African crude said.
That leaves more West African crude for the U.S. market and less need for North Sea grades such as Brent to cross the Atlantic.
Urals in the Mediterranean continued to hold firm as refiners there, working on a low stock basis, now find themselves short of crude, traders said.

Planned maintenance on some of the berths at Novorossiisk, as well as frequent closures due to bad weather, has led to a relatively tight supply situation. Some Mediterranean traders expected barrels from the May Kirkuk loading schedule to be cancelled due to the recent rise in crude prices.
"Some of what (Kirkuk) is expected to load has to be seriously under threat as it's a dollar and cent deal not a barrel deal," one trader said referring to the U.N. oil-for-food agreement.
